title: Rajab: the prayer's gift
tomorrow: the month people forget. why did he fast so much of it?

cards: A break at work comes with a timer: fifteen minutes, then back, and it's easy to spend them scrolling.

In Rajab, some Muslims remember a night when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was carried from Mecca to Jerusalem and, the reports add, up through the heavens. He came back down with one gift for his people. Not a book.

teach.b: The Qur'an opens the story in Pickthall's words: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship."
The reports in Sahih al-Bukhari tell the rest: the ascent, and the prayers given to him there. Scholars differ on which month the night fell in; Rajab is where some communities remember it.
Earlier in this block you met the bargaining from fifty down to five.
Today's question is different: is prayer a duty, or a gift? The reports lean toward gift.
In Sunan Abi Dawud, when the time came, the Prophet would say to Bilal: call the prayer, and give us rest with it. Not rest from it. Rest with it.
In Sunan an-Nasa'i, he says the coolness of his eyes was placed in prayer. Now a neighbor.
The Hebrew Bible tells of Daniel, far from home, who went into his house, where the windows faced Jerusalem, and knelt three times a day, prayed and gave thanks, as he had always done.
The Talmud learns from him that a person prays three times a day. What's shared: prayer at set times, turned toward a holy place, a day built around turning to God.
What's honestly different: Daniel kneels three times toward Jerusalem; Muslims pray five times toward the Ka'ba in Mecca, with their own words and movements. Neither is a copy of the other.
That's the gift of prayer: a rest set into the day.

how: In Rajab some Muslim communities hold talks and gatherings recalling the Night Journey and Ascension (al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj), while others mark no special night; all keep the five daily prayers the reports say were given then.

games.q: your Jewish friend says she prays three times a day, like Daniel, facing Jerusalem. you pray five, facing Mecca. what's a fair way to put it?
o: we share set prayer times and a holy direction; the times and places differ.
it's all the same thing really, just with different numbers.
five is more than three, so ours is the stronger practice.
games.why: Daniel kneels three times toward Jerusalem; Muslims pray five times toward the Ka'ba. shared: set times and a direction. different: the count, the place, the words. neither is ranked.

practice: Stand, if you can, feet planted and hands loose at your sides. Turn toward a window or a quiet wall, as if facing somewhere that matters. Then lower yourself slowly to sit, and let the rest of the sit be rest: not a task, a break.
If you pray, let this be the stillness before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Rajab: a sacred month in which some communities remember the Night Journey, and with it the gift of the five prayers.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj, the Night Journey and the Ascension.

carryVoice: Keep this near: the gift of prayer is a rest set into the day, not a chore cut out of it. Six of fourteen.
